questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A literary work written to be performed on stage by actors is called
questions.explanation: Drama is the literary form specifically composed for performance, using dialogue and action rather than narration.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The character flaw or error in judgement that leads to a tragic hero's downfall is called
questions.explanation: Hamartia refers to the fatal flaw or mistake in a tragic protagonist's character that sets their downfall in motion.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Excessive pride or overconfidence that often leads a tragic hero to defy fate or the gods is called
questions.explanation: Hubris describes extreme arrogance or pride, frequently the root cause of a tragic hero's hamartia and eventual downfall.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The emotional release or purging of pity and fear experienced by the audience at the end of a tragedy is called
questions.explanation: Catharsis, a concept from Aristotle, describes the cleansing emotional effect tragedy has on its audience through pity and fear.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A speech delivered by a character alone on stage, revealing their inner thoughts to the audience, is called a
questions.explanation: A soliloquy is spoken by a character alone (or believing themselves alone), giving the audience direct insight into their private thoughts.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A brief remark made by a character, heard by the audience but not by other characters on stage, is called an
questions.explanation: An aside is a short comment directed to the audience, conventionally unheard by other characters present in the scene.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A long, uninterrupted speech by one character addressed to other characters or the audience is called a
questions.explanation: A monologue is an extended speech by a single character, which, unlike a soliloquy, may be addressed to other characters present.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A situation in drama where the audience knows something important that a character on stage does not know is called
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony creates tension by allowing the audience to understand the true significance of events or words that a character misunderstands.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The sequence of events in a play, encompassing the arrangement of incidents and conflicts, is called the
questions.explanation: Plot refers to the structured sequence of events, typically including exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, and resolution.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The time and place in which the events of a play occur is called the
questions.explanation: Setting establishes the temporal and geographical context of a drama, often shaping its mood and the characters' circumstances.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The process by which a playwright creates and develops the personalities of the people in a play is called
questions.explanation: Characterization is the method an author uses to reveal a character's traits, motivations, and personality through action, speech, and description.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The technique of creating tension or anticipation in the audience about what will happen next is called
questions.explanation: Suspense is deliberately built by the playwright to keep the audience anxious or curious about the unfolding outcome of events.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The final resolution of the plot, where loose ends are tied up after the climax, is called the
questions.explanation: The denouement (French for 'unknotting') is the concluding part of a play, resolving the conflicts introduced earlier in the plot.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The part of a play that introduces the characters, setting, and background information is called the
questions.explanation: Exposition sets the stage at the beginning of a play, providing the audience with necessary background before the conflict develops.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The turning point or moment of highest tension in a play's plot is called the
questions.explanation: The climax marks the peak of dramatic tension, typically the point at which the central conflict reaches its decisive turn.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The events leading up to the climax of a play, in which tension builds, are collectively called the
questions.explanation: Rising action consists of the complications and events that build tension from the exposition toward the climax.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The events that follow the climax, showing the consequences of the central conflict's resolution, are called the
questions.explanation: Falling action depicts how the story unwinds after the climax, leading toward the final resolution (denouement).

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A struggle between opposing forces in a play, which drives the plot forward, is called
questions.explanation: Conflict, whether between characters, within a character, or against outside forces, is the central engine driving dramatic action.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A conflict that occurs within a single character's own mind, such as a struggle over a difficult decision, is called
questions.explanation: Internal conflict occurs entirely within a character, often involving competing desires, values, or emotions.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A conflict between a character and an outside force, such as another character, society, or nature, is called
questions.explanation: External conflict pits a character against forces outside themselves, including other characters, society, or the natural world.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A minor character included mainly to draw a contrast that highlights the traits of a main character is called a
questions.explanation: A foil is a character whose qualities contrast with those of another character, usually the protagonist, to sharpen the audience's understanding of both.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The central character around whom the main action of a play revolves is called the
questions.explanation: The protagonist is the principal character whose goals and struggles drive the central conflict of the play.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The character or force that opposes the protagonist in a play is called the
questions.explanation: The antagonist creates the central opposition to the protagonist, generating the conflict that propels the plot.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A secondary storyline running alongside the main plot of a play, often reflecting or contrasting with it, is called a
questions.explanation: A subplot is a secondary line of action that develops alongside and often reinforces the themes or events of the main plot.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A group of performers in classical drama who comment on the action and reflect public opinion is called the
questions.explanation: The chorus, especially prominent in classical Greek drama, provides commentary, background, and moral reflection on the unfolding events.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A long fictional narrative, typically divided into chapters, is called a
questions.explanation: A novel is an extended work of prose fiction, usually with a complex plot and multiple characters developed over many chapters.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A short piece of fictional prose, usually focused on a single incident or a small set of characters, is called a
questions.explanation: A short story is a brief work of fiction, generally more focused in scope and length than a novel.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Non-fiction prose that presents facts, real events, or the writer's own experiences is called
questions.explanation: Non-fiction prose is based on real events, facts, or genuine experience, distinguishing it from invented fictional narratives.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A story told using 'I' or 'we', from the point of view of a character within the story, is written in
questions.explanation: A first-person narrator participates in the story and relates events using 'I' or 'we', offering a limited, personal viewpoint.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A narrative perspective in which the narrator knows the thoughts and feelings of all characters is called
questions.explanation: A third-person omniscient narrator has unrestricted access to the thoughts, feelings, and motivations of every character in the story.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A narrative perspective restricted to the thoughts and experiences of only one character, told using 'he' or 'she', is called
questions.explanation: Third-person limited narration follows one character's perspective closely, without direct access to other characters' inner thoughts.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The central message, idea, or insight about life that a work of prose conveys is called its
questions.explanation: Theme is the underlying idea or message a writer explores through the events, characters, and conflicts of a narrative.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An author's distinctive way of using language, sentence structure, and tone in a work is called their
questions.explanation: Style encompasses an author's particular choices in diction, sentence construction, and tone, giving a work its distinctive voice.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A recurring element, such as an image, idea, or situation, that helps to develop a work's central theme is called a
questions.explanation: A motif is a recurring symbolic element that reinforces or develops a text's larger themes throughout the narrative.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The underlying reasons that drive a character to behave in a particular way in a story are called their
questions.explanation: Character motivation explains the psychological or circumstantial reasons behind a character's actions and decisions.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A character who remains essentially unchanged throughout a story is called a
questions.explanation: A static character's personality and outlook stay largely the same from the beginning to the end of the narrative.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A character who undergoes significant internal change or growth over the course of a story is called a
questions.explanation: A dynamic character experiences meaningful development or transformation as the plot unfolds.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A character defined by only one or two traits, without much complexity or depth, is called a
questions.explanation: A flat character is simply and briefly sketched, typically embodying a single dominant trait rather than a fully developed personality.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A character portrayed with the complexity, depth, and contradictions of a real person is called a
questions.explanation: A round character is fully developed, often multi-dimensional, with believable strengths, flaws, and inner conflicts.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The organisation of events in a narrative according to the order in which they actually happen is called
questions.explanation: Chronological structure presents events in the sequence in which they occur, from earliest to latest.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A technique in which a narrative interrupts its present action to show events from an earlier time is called a
questions.explanation: A flashback shifts the narrative back in time to reveal past events relevant to the present story.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A technique in which a writer hints at events that will happen later in the story is called
questions.explanation: Foreshadowing plants early clues or hints that prepare the reader for events that will occur later in the narrative.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A story that begins in the middle of the action, with earlier events explained later, is said to begin
questions.explanation: In medias res, Latin for 'into the middle of things', describes a narrative technique that plunges the reader directly into ongoing action.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A struggle in prose fiction between a character and society's expectations or rules is an example of
options: conflict between the individual and society
questions.explanation: This type of external conflict pits a character's personal desires or values against the norms, laws, or expectations of the wider society.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The physical, historical, and social environment in which a novel's events take place is called its
questions.explanation: Setting situates a narrative in a particular place, time period, and social context, shaping the characters' circumstances and choices.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A group of lines forming a unit within a poem, similar to a paragraph in prose, is called a
questions.explanation: A stanza is a set of lines grouped together, forming one of the structural building blocks of a poem.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The pattern of similar-sounding word endings at the end of lines in a poem is called its
questions.explanation: Rhyme scheme describes the ordered pattern of end rhymes across the lines of a poem, often labelled with letters like ABAB.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of poetry is called its
questions.explanation: Meter refers to the structured rhythm created by patterns of stressed and unstressed syllables within a poem's lines.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The repetition of the same consonant sound at the beginning of neighbouring words is called
questions.explanation: Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds across nearby words, as in 'wild and windy weather'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The repetition of similar vowel sounds in nearby words, without the words necessarily rhyming, is called
questions.explanation: Assonance repeats vowel sounds within words in close proximity, as in 'the rain in Spain'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The repetition of similar consonant sounds, especially at the end of words, in close proximity is called
questions.explanation: Consonance repeats consonant sounds, often at the middle or end of words, as in 'pitter-patter'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The use of words that imitate the natural sound of the thing they describe is called
questions.explanation: Onomatopoeia uses words whose pronunciation mimics real-world sounds, such as 'buzz', 'hiss', or 'clang'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Language that appeals vividly to the senses, helping a reader visualise or otherwise sensorially experience a poem, is called
questions.explanation: Imagery uses descriptive, sensory language to create vivid mental pictures and appeal to sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech that directly describes one thing as being another, without using 'like' or 'as', is called a
questions.explanation: A metaphor makes an implicit, direct comparison, asserting that one thing literally is another to highlight a shared quality.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech that compares two unlike things using the words 'like' or 'as' is called a
questions.explanation: A simile draws an explicit comparison between two different things, using connecting words such as 'like' or 'as'.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech that gives human qualities or actions to non-human things or abstract ideas is called
questions.explanation: Personification attributes human characteristics, emotions, or actions to objects, animals, or abstract concepts.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech combining two contradictory terms for effect, such as 'deafening silence', is called an
questions.explanation: An oxymoron places two seemingly opposite words side by side to create a striking, often thought-provoking effect.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A statement that seems self-contradictory or absurd but may reveal an underlying truth is called a
questions.explanation: A paradox appears logically contradictory on the surface, yet often expresses a deeper or more complex truth upon reflection.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech that uses deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or effect is called
questions.explanation: Hyperbole exaggerates a statement well beyond literal truth to emphasise a point or create a strong impression.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech in which the actual meaning of words is different from, or opposite to, their literal meaning is called
questions.explanation: Irony conveys a meaning that contrasts with, or is opposite to, the literal or expected meaning of the words used.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech in which a part of something is used to represent the whole, or the whole represents a part, is called
questions.explanation: Synecdoche uses a part of something to stand for the entire thing (e.g., 'all hands on deck' meaning all crew members).

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A figure of speech in which something closely associated with a thing is used to represent that thing is called
questions.explanation: Metonymy substitutes the name of something with a closely related term (e.g., 'the crown' referring to the monarchy).

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The overall emotional atmosphere created by a poem for its reader is called its
questions.explanation: Mood refers to the emotional atmosphere or feeling that a poem evokes in its readers.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The poet's attitude toward the subject matter or audience, as conveyed through word choice and style, is called
questions.explanation: Tone reflects the poet's own attitude toward the subject, distinct from mood, which is the feeling evoked in the reader.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The voice or character through whom a poem is narrated, who may or may not be the poet, is called the
questions.explanation: The persona, or speaker, is the voice used in a poem, which readers should not automatically assume is the poet's own.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A poem consisting of fourteen lines, often with a specific rhyme scheme, is called a
questions.explanation: A sonnet is a fixed fourteen-line poem, commonly written in forms such as the Shakespearean or Petrarchan sonnet, each with its own rhyme scheme.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A formal poem written to mourn or reflect on the death of a person is called an
questions.explanation: An elegy is a reflective, often mournful poem composed to lament and honour someone who has died.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A poem that celebrates or addresses a particular subject in an elevated, formal style is called an
questions.explanation: An ode is a formal, often lyrical poem that praises or reflects deeply on a particular person, object, or idea.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A poem that tells a story, often in simple stanzas and originally meant to be sung, is called a
questions.explanation: A ballad is a narrative poem, traditionally passed down orally or through song, often recounting dramatic or romantic events.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A long narrative poem celebrating the deeds of a legendary or heroic figure is called an
questions.explanation: An epic is an extended narrative poem recounting the grand adventures and achievements of a heroic protagonist.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A poem or section of verse with no fixed rhyme scheme or regular meter is described as
questions.explanation: Free verse abandons consistent meter and rhyme, allowing the poet greater flexibility in rhythm and line structure.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Unrhymed poetry written in a regular meter, especially iambic pentameter, is called
questions.explanation: Blank verse follows a consistent metrical pattern (commonly iambic pentameter) but does not use end rhyme.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The repetition of a word, phrase, or line at intervals throughout a poem, especially in songs and ballads, is called a
questions.explanation: A refrain is a recurring line or phrase, often repeated at the end of each stanza, reinforcing the poem's central mood or message.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The continuation of a sentence or clause from one line of poetry to the next without a pause is called
questions.explanation: Enjambment carries a thought across a line break without terminal punctuation, creating flow and momentum in the reading.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A strong pause or break occurring within a line of poetry, often marked by punctuation, is called a
questions.explanation: A caesura is a deliberate pause within a line of verse, often used for emphasis or to reflect natural speech rhythm.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A poetic device that repeats a word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines or clauses for emphasis is called
questions.explanation: Anaphora repeats the same word or phrase at the start of consecutive lines or sentences to build rhetorical emphasis.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Understatement that deliberately presents something as less significant than it actually is, often for ironic effect, is called
questions.explanation: Litotes (a form of meiosis) is a deliberate understatement, often using a negative to express a positive, for subtle or ironic effect.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A direct address to an absent person, an abstract idea, or an inanimate object as though it could respond is called
questions.explanation: Apostrophe involves addressing someone absent, deceased, or something non-human directly, as if it could hear and respond.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The use of a symbol, in poetry or prose, involves
options: repeating consonant sounds for rhythmic effect
describing one thing directly as another
using an object, person, or place to represent an idea or concept beyond its literal meaning
creating a pause within a line of verse
questions.explanation: A symbol carries meaning beyond its literal, concrete identity, often standing for a broader abstract idea, emotion, or theme.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Allusion, as a literary device, refers to
options: an indirect reference to another well-known work, person, or event
a technique of describing sensory experiences
a fourteen-line poem with a fixed rhyme scheme
the sound pattern created by repeating consonants
questions.explanation: Allusion briefly references a familiar work, historical event, or figure, relying on the reader's knowledge to add deeper meaning.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Literature can generally be classified into which three broad forms?
options: novel, short story, and epic only
questions.explanation: The three broad traditional forms of literature are drama (performed), prose (narrative fiction/non-fiction), and poetry (verse).

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A play in which the protagonist experiences a serious downfall, often due to a tragic flaw, and the ending is sorrowful, is called a
questions.explanation: Tragedy centres on a protagonist's serious misfortune or downfall, frequently resulting from a fatal character flaw.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A play written primarily to amuse the audience, typically with a happy ending, is called a
questions.explanation: Comedy aims to entertain and amuse, generally resolving its conflicts with a happy or satisfying conclusion.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A play that combines serious and comic elements, often reflecting on the complexities of life, is sometimes classified as a
questions.explanation: Tragicomedy blends tragic and comic elements within a single work, resisting a purely tragic or purely comic classification.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The comparison of a work's themes to real-life or historical events, showing relevance beyond the text itself, is a key part of
options: counting the number of characters in a play
questions.explanation: A strong literary analysis connects a text's themes to broader real-world, historical, or social contexts, deepening understanding of its significance.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: When analysing a character's development across a play or novel, a student should pay close attention to
options: only the number of times the character speaks
how the character's actions, speech, and relationships change over the course of the work
only the setting in which the character first appears
only the character's name and physical appearance
questions.explanation: Character analysis requires tracking a character's evolving actions, motivations, and relationships throughout the narrative, not just surface details.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A recurring social concern often explored in African drama and prose, involving tension between traditional customs and modern Western influence, is called
questions.explanation: Culture conflict, a common theme in African literature, examines the clash between indigenous traditions and imported Western values or systems.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A recurring theme in literature concerning the abuse of power or bribery by those in government is
questions.explanation: Political corruption is a widely explored theme, especially in African literature, critiquing the misuse of power for personal gain.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The philosophical theme exploring whether events are predetermined or shaped by a character's own choices is called
questions.explanation: This theme examines the tension between destiny (fate) and a character's capacity to shape their own future through choice.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A recurring theme addressing the roles, expectations, or struggles faced by men and women within a society is called
questions.explanation: Gender dynamics as a literary theme explores how societal expectations shape and constrain the roles of men and women.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: An author's exploration of a character's search for self-understanding or a sense of belonging is commonly discussed under the theme of
questions.explanation: Identity as a literary theme concerns a character's quest to understand who they are, often shaped by culture, history, or personal experience.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: When studying a Shakespearean play, understanding archaic vocabulary and grammatical forms unfamiliar to modern readers falls under the study of
questions.explanation: Shakespeare's plays were written in Elizabethan English, requiring familiarity with archaic vocabulary, grammar, and idiom to fully understand the text.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A subplot in a Shakespearean play often serves to
options: remove the need for a resolution in the main plot
confuse the audience with unrelated events
mirror, contrast with, or comment on the themes of the main plot
questions.explanation: Subplots frequently parallel or contrast with the main plot, reinforcing or complicating the play's central themes.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: When analysing a poem, identifying the number of stanzas, lines per stanza, and rhyme pattern is part of examining its
questions.explanation: A poem's structural layout, including stanza count and rhyme pattern, is a key formal element considered in poetic analysis.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Determining who is speaking in a poem, and whether that voice reflects the poet's own views, is part of identifying the
questions.explanation: Identifying the persona helps readers understand whose perspective and voice shape the poem's meaning, which may differ from the poet's own views.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: Symbolism in a novel refers to the author's use of
options: only rhyming words at the end of each chapter
objects, characters, or events to represent deeper meanings beyond their literal significance
questions.explanation: Symbolism allows an author to embed deeper thematic meaning within concrete elements of the narrative, such as objects or recurring images.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A shift in a novel's structure, such as a sudden change in narrative perspective or time period, is often analysed to reveal
options: the physical size of the book
the price at which the book was sold
only errors made by the author
how the author manipulates structure to affect meaning, pace, or perspective
questions.explanation: Structural shifts, such as changes in narration or chronology, are deliberate authorial choices that can affect how meaning and tension are conveyed.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: When comparing a major character to a minor character in a play or novel, the analysis usually focuses on
options: the number of scenes set outdoors
their relative importance to the plot and how they influence or reflect on each other
which character has the longer name
questions.explanation: Comparing major and minor characters typically considers their narrative weight and how minor characters support, contrast with, or reveal major ones.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: The 'mood' evoked by a piece of prose fiction is best assessed by examining
options: only the number of chapters in the novel
only the publication date of the novel
the atmosphere created through setting, word choice, and descriptive detail
only the price of the book
questions.explanation: Mood in prose, as in poetry, is shaped by the writer's descriptive choices, setting, and overall atmosphere conveyed to the reader.

questions.subject: Literature in English
questions.text: A close, line-by-line reading of a poem, examining word choice, imagery, and structure in detail, is generally referred to as
questions.explanation: Close reading of poetry involves a detailed, careful examination of language, imagery, and form to uncover layered meanings.
